https://www.kyivpost.com/post/82010.text: War Ukraine World North America Latin America Europe Eastern Europe Middle East Africa Asia Economy Business Technology Finance Energy Agriculture Videos Podcasts Analysis Corruption Watch Opinions Culture Reviews History Sports Classifieds Spotlight Cartoons EN UK Belarus Lukashenko Belarusian Opposition Moves to Hold Lukashenko Regime Accountable over Ukraine War In brief: The Belarusian opposition is preparing to hand Ukraine a “consolidated body of evidence” it says shows the Alexander Lukashenko regime has been complicit in Russia’s aggression against Ukraine since 2022, as part of efforts to hold Minsk accountable. by TVP World | Aug. 9, 2026, 11:35 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Belarus' President Alexander Lukashenko attends a meeting with his Russian counterpart in Volgograd on April 29, 2025. (Photo by Alexander KAZAKOV / POOL / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip The material will be submitted to Ukraine’s foreign ministry and Prosecutor General’s Office, Pavel Latushka, deputy head of the Belarusian opposition’s government-in-exile , told Polish state news agency PAP. Experts working with the exiled Belarusian opposition presented evidence at a meeting on Friday which they said documented the Lukashenko regime ’s involvement in Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, PAP reported. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “We are preparing a consolidated body of evidence [...] which we hope will be used as part of an investigation to be launched within the framework of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine,” Latushka said. The planned tribunal is intended to investigate and prosecute senior officials responsible for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, filling a gap in the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. Advertisement In May, 36 countries and the European Union signed an agreement establishing a management committee that will oversee the tribunal’s organizational launch, including its budget and administrative structure. Latushka urged democratic countries to move quickly with the ratification process needed for the body to begin its work. Latushka, who is now based in Warsaw, served as Belarus’s ambassador to Poland from 2002 to 2008 before later breaking with the Lukashenko regime and joining the opposition. Other Topics of Interest ‘Putin’s Defeat in Ukraine Necessary for a Free Belarus,’ Exiled Opposition Leader Says The defeat of Russian President Vladimir Putin in his war against Ukraine is necessary for Belarus to become free of the pro-Kremlin regime in Minsk, Belarus’s exiled opposition leader has said. How Belarus aided Moscow Belarusian opposition groups have long accused Lukashenko, a key ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, of enabling the Kremlin’s full-scale of Ukraine by allowing Belarusian territory and infrastructure to be used by Moscow’s forces. Russian troops entered northern Ukraine from Belarus when the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, while Russian aircraft and missiles have also operated from Belarusian territory. Latushka said Belarusian democratic forces want Lukashenko held accountable for alleged complicity in Russia’s aggression, as well as crimes against humanity and alleged war crimes linked to the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territories to Belarus and their subsequent indoctrination. Advertisement Crackdown at home Latushka also called on other countries to support Lithuania’s referral of Belarus to the International Criminal Court over alleged forced deportations and the persecution of civil society and political opponents. Lithuania referred the situation to the court in September 2024, and the ICC opened an investigation into possible crimes against humanity committed by the Belarusian regime in March 2026. The repression intensified following Belarus’s disputed 2020 presidential election, which handed Lukashenko another term in office and sparked mass protests across the country. Between 300,000 and 500,000 Belarusians are estimated to have fled the country following the crackdown, according to a 2023 report by the Council of Europe. Latushka told PAP that Polish authorities had so far not joined Lithuania in supporting the referral. Picture: iStock/Nataliia Hruts FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 11 Live Music Siblings Duncan and Rona Macleod of Bonar Bridge bring a wealth of traditional music and song to Durness Village Hall on Friday from 7.30pm. A Blas Festival event. Tickets £5-£38; pay what you can. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 12 Car Boot Sale Car boot sale at Dornoch Community Centre (Social Club) on Saturday 9.30am-12.30pm. Community Market North Coast Market at Bettyhill Hall on Saturday 11am-3pm. Food and craft stalls. Run by the Bettyhill Hall Committee. Community Market Golspie Community Market at Fountain Road Hall on Saturday 11am-3pm. A variety of local food and craft stalls. Cinema Community Cinema screening at Timespan Museum and Arts Centre, Helmsdale, on Saturday 11am-1pm. The film to be screened is the 2018 environmental documentary Grit, co-directed by Cynthia Wade and Sasha Friedlander. The 80-minute film focuses on the human and environmental devastation caused by an industrial disaster in East Java, Indonesia. FILM Halladale Film Club screening of the comedy-drama Rental Family at Halladale Community Hall (seven miles south of Melvich along the A897) on Saturday 7pm-10pm. Screenings are followed by tea, coffee, home bakes and a chance to chat. Non-members £5/£4/£2. Race Night Melvich and Portskerra Hall Committee presents a Race Night fundraiser at Strathy Hall on Saturday. Doors open 6.30pm for a 7.30pm start. BYOB LIVE MUSIC Capercaillie and Session A9 fiddle player Charlie McKerron and friends perform at Dornoch Cathedral on Saturday 7.30pm-9.30pm. Featuring Ross Ainslie, Marc Clement and Cailean McKerron. Tickets £20pp from the Dornoch Gatherings website. SUNDAY, SEPTEMBER 13 Tree Seed Collecting Day Tree Seed Collecting Day at Assynt on Sunday 10am-4pm. Join Chris Goodman, a ranger with the Woodland Trust Scotland, and Roz Birch, from Trees for Life, at Glencanisp for a day in the wood collecting tree seeds, berries and nuts, and learning about Scotland’s rain forest. A free event, minimum age 12. Book via Eventbrite or for further information, email: chrisgoodman@woodlandtrust.org.uk. Raven’s Rock Assynt Field Club excursion to Raven’s Rock Gorge and Nature Trail, near Rosehall, on Sunday 10.30am-2pm. Meet at the Highland Council car park behind the Culag Hotel, Lochinver, at 10.30am to facilitate the sharing of transport. Bring lunch, waterproofs and good footwear. A free event. For more information, contact: Jane Livingston on 07460 532253. Duck Race East Sutherland Rotary Club’s 2026 Charity Duck Race at Brora Bridge on Sunday 3pm for 3.30pm. Prizes for top three ducks plus consolation prizes. Free BBQ at the finish line. A fundraiser for youth and children’s projects in East Sutherland. MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 14 Live Music The Budapest Cafe Orchestra takes its Goulash in the Glen Grand Scottish Tour 2026 to Rogart Mart on Monday (September 14). Doors open 7pm for a 7.30pm start.BYOB Tickets on the door or via Ticketsource; £17/£10 (u16). TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 15 Lecture Tain and District Field Club lecture on Tuesday in the Minor Hall of the Duthac Centre, Tain, from 7.30pm. Fraser Symonds will give a talk titled ‘Patagonia: Land of the Puma. Tea, coffee and conversation after each lecture. THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 17 Coffee and a Blether Coffee and a Blether at Rogart Village Hall on Thursday 10am-12pm. Meet and Eat Meet and Eat at the Kyle Centre, Tongue, on Thursday. Drop in from 12pm-2pm. On the menu is baked potato and toppings.£5pp. It is advisable to check in advance to ensure that the events listed are going ahead as planned. https://www.byui.edu/newsroom/categories.text: Developing Disciples Inspired Education Career-Ready Announcements Campus Events 25 Years Search Developing Disciples Inspired Education Career-Ready Announcements Campus Events 25 Years Search Teaching English Abroad, Learning to Lead Long before graduation, BYU-Idaho students in the TESOL program are leading classrooms of their own, and discovering what mentorship makes possible. Ashley Bednar was the only English teacher for an entire class of young adults in Czechia this summer—14 classes, plus test prep, lesson planning, one-on-one tutoring and feedback, with no second teacher to share the load. It was intimidating, she admits, especially at first. Bednar was one of several BYU-Idaho students who traveled across the world this summer to teach English through the university’s Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) program, teaching at Cumorah Academy. Long before they finish a degree, TESOL students take on the kind of leadership a real classroom demands, and Bednar traces the confidence to walk into hers alone back to a habit she built on campus: showing up to office hours. “At BYUI, I [developed] a pattern of creating relationships with mentors like Don Hansen,” Bednar said. “I would go to his office hours, we would talk about things, and he [even] helped me with my application.” Hansen, the BYU-Idaho Department Chair who oversees the TESOL program, was one of the faculty members Bednar credited with helping her get accepted. When she faced challenges in Czechia, Bednar reached for that same habit and turned to her Cumorah Academy supervisor for help. “Being able to have [a] mentor was incredible,” Bednar said. “I knew that asking somebody to mentor me wasn’t going to create an unnecessary burden on them because I knew I could also bring things to the table.... BYU-Idaho prepared me to not be afraid to ask for help.” Throughout the summer, Bednar and her supervisor built a system of lesson planning and feedback. Putting her own ideas and decisions into practice week after week helped her gain confidence in both her decisions and her teaching. That impact became clear as she continued to hear from former students in Czechia. “About half of them have reached out to me and told me that they have better jobs now because of their English,” Bednar said. “Some of them have taken English certification tests through Cambridge … and they’ve passed!” The experience was equally impactful and educational for Elise Jensen, an elementary education major who first heard about the opportunity almost by accident. “I was at my apartment, done with homework, and got an email [about an] opportunity to teach English in Taiwan,” she said. “I was like, ‘you know what? What harm is going to come from applying for this?’” she added. Jensen taught in Taiwan in 2023 and in 2026 returned to Asia to teach in Japan, where she saw firsthand how students’ confidence grew alongside their language skills. “It was just amazing to see how… [they not only progressed] in their English proficiency, but their confidence in themselves and their abilities as well,” she said. “Watching that growth in them was amazing.” Both Bednar and Jensen say while going off to a foreign country and teaching English on your own may sound intimidating, BYU-Idaho faculty will prepare participants to teach and lead. “It’s so worth it,” Jensen said. “You’re not going to know everything, but you do know enough.” Before sending students abroad, Hansen and his team carefully vet each site to ensure safety and proximity to a temple so students can live their faith. Establishing these international partnerships relies heavily on word of mouth, conferences, and organic connections—a rigorous process well worth the effort for the unique leadership opportunities and growth it offers students. “I see them leading a classroom,” Hansen said. “They’re doing it. And the sense of accomplishment they get from that is really, really rewarding.” Hansen remarked on the benefits of the program, not just for the students teaching English, but for those learning it as well. “This is the ultimate win, win, win,” Hansen said. “It’s good for my students, it’s good for their students, and I think it’s good for the world for people to really get to see each other up close.” For more information about BYU-Idaho's TESOL program visit https://www.byui.edu/languages-international-studies/tesol Tags Student Stories

https://www.dw.com/en/bulgarians-vote-in.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ouwb Prefer DW on Google Bulgaria remains sharply divided over its ties with Moscow Image: Stoyan Nenov/REUTERS Advertisement Bulgarians on Sunday began voting in a highly contested presidential runoff following a tight race between the two main contenders last weekend. The November 1 runoff pits two competing visions of Bulgaria against each other. Moscow-friendly incumbent Iliana Yotova opposes military aid to Ukraine , while former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov is backed by the pro-Western opposition. In last Sunday's first round, which saw voter turnout fall to a historic low, Yotova won with 34.76% of the vote, less than three percentage points ahead of Gyurov with 31.95%. Iliana Yotova (left) beat Andrey Gyurov (right) by a narrow margin in the first round on October 25, 2026 Image: BGNES Although Bulgaria's presidency has largely ceremonial duties, the president can appoint interim governments during political crises, serve as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and veto legislation. Ukraine war divides Bulgaria The war in Ukraine has become a central issue in the election, with voters heading to the polls amid growing security concerns in the Black Sea , which borders Bulgaria, following a rise in drone attacks targeting commercial vessels. How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Yotova has presented herself as a "president of peace" who favors dialogue with Moscow. In a TV debate before the runoff, Gyurov accused Yotova of avoiding direct criticism of Russia over the Black Sea attacks . " Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken. Let us name the country from which the threats are coming," he said. In response, Yotova argued that "peace can come only through negotiations," and maintained that continued aid for Ukraine "leads only to more destruction and the deaths of many people on both sides." Yotova vs Gyurov: Between Russia and the West If elected, Yotova is expected to pursue a similar approach to Prime Minister Rumen Radev — keeping Bulgaria on its European path while seeking closer ties with Russia and advocating the lifting of sanctions . A victory would make Yotova the first woman to be elected president of Bulgaria [FILE: October 25, 2026] Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance Her opponent Gyurov previously served as deputy governor of Bulgaria's central bank and as caretaker prime minister, leading the country in early 2026. He has repeatedly voiced strong support for Ukraine and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership. After the first round of voting, Gyurov said that Bulgaria faced a choice "between two personalities, two directions, and two ways of exercising presidential powers."
